2                I.   INTRODUCTION AND PURPOSE OF REBUTTAL TESTIMONY

3    Q.   ARE YOU THE SAME CORIN E. COOLEY WHO PRESENTED DIRECT

4         TESTIMONY ON BEHALF OF ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY LLC

5         (“ONCOR”) AND LCRA TRANSMISSION SERVICES CORPORATION ("LCRA

6         TSC," AND TOGETHER WITH ONCOR, THE "APPLICANTS") IN THIS

7         DOCKET?

8    A.   Yes.

9    Q.   HAVE YOU REVIEWED THE DIRECT TESTIMONY OF INTERVENORS AND

10        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS (“COMMISSION”) STAFF?

11   A.   Yes, I have.

12   Q.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

13   A.   The purpose of my rebuttal testimony is to respond to the testimony filed by the

14        parties to this proceeding regarding the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill

15        Substation 765 kilovolt (“kV”) transmission line project (“Proposed Transmission

16        Line Project”), for which Applicants seek approval in this proceeding.      More

17        specifically, I respond to certain engineering-related statements and concerns

18        raised in intervenor direct testimony regarding topics such as Applicants’

19        construction and safety practices, design of the Proposed Transmission Line

20        Project, and land use constraints.

 1               II.    REBUTTAL REGARDING HEALTH AND SAFETY CONCERNS

2    Q.   THE DIRECT TESTIMONIES OF INTERVENORS SUCH AS LARRY MARTIN

3         (PAGE 14, LINES 14 THROUGH 18) AND KAREN AND STEVE MCCOURY, ON

4         BEHALF OF THEMSELVES AND CHEROKEE CREEK PARTNERS (PAGE 12,

5         LINES 22 THROUGH 26), EXPRESS GENERAL CONCERNS ABOUT

6         TRANSMISSION LINES PRODUCING ELECTRIC AND MAGNETIC FIELDS

7         (“EMF”). HOW DO APPLICANTS MITIGATE POTENTIAL EFFECTS OF EMF

8         PRODUCED BY ITS TRANSMISSION LINES?

9    A.   Applicants minimize potential EMF effects by designing the Proposed

10        Transmission Line Project to maintain appropriate right-of-way (“ROW”) width

11        consistent with field strength and by increasing phase to ground distance. At the

12        edge of the ROW, EMF levels from the Proposed Transmission Line Project will

13        be comparable to common household appliances and considerably less than many

14        electronic devices we expose ourselves to on a frequent basis.

15               Potential EMF impacts are also mitigated by routing the Proposed

16        Transmission Line Project to comply with the Commission’s policy of prudent

17        avoidance.    Applicants’ witness Ms. Casey D. Petty discusses in her direct

18        testimony that all filed routes for the Proposed Transmission Line Project comply

19        with this policy. The rebuttal testimony of Applicants’ witness Dr. Edward P.

20        Gelmann offers his independent expert opinion regarding alleged potential health

21        risks of extra high voltage transmission lines.

 1    Q.   VARIOUS INTERVENORS, INCLUDING PAUL GRIMME, ON BEHALF OF

2         BERNAREGGIO FAMILY PARTNERS, LTD. (PAGE 21, LINES 1 THROUGH 11)

3         AND KURT POOLE, ON BEHALF OF 2-K POOLE RANCHES, LP (PAGES 2-3),

4         SUBMITTED TESTIMONY VOICING GENERAL HEALTH AND SAFETY

5         CONCERNS FOR PEOPLE AND ANIMALS LIVING NEAR OR TRAVELING

6         UNDER THE PROPOSED TRANSMISSION LINE. SIMILARLY, INTERVENORS

7         SUCH AS JAMES ACOSTA (PAGE 5) EXPRESSED SAFETY CONCERNS

8         ABOUT LIGHTNING OCCURRING NEAR TRANSMISSION LINES AND OTHER

9         POTENTIAL FIRE HAZARDS POSED BY TRANSMISSION LINES, INCLUDING

10        ELECTRICAL ARCING RISKS. HOW DO APPLICANTS ADDRESS SAFETY

11        AND FIRE-RELATED CONCERNS SUCH AS THESE?

12   A.   Applicants have extensive experience safely operating electric infrastructure

13        across Texas in areas where people live, work, and play on a daily basis.

14        Applicants’ practices and experience have proven very effective in addressing

15        potential safety hazards. Applicants design, construct, operate, and maintain their

16        respective facilities in accordance with all governing rules and regulations,

17        including the National Electrical Safety Code (“NESC”), to prevent and mitigate

18        potential safety hazards, and Applicants’ ROW-maintenance and vegetation-

19        management practices are designed to further mitigate potential safety concerns.

20              Applicants will maintain the minimum clearances prescribed by industry

21        standards, such as the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (“OSHA”)

22        minimum approach distances to energized electric lines, to ensure personnel

 1         safety during construction. In addition to the NESC and OSHA, Applicants also

2         adhere to the American National Standards Institute (“ANSI”), Institute of Electrical

3         and Electronics Engineers (“IEEE”), and other national standards providing

4         specific requirements for insulation levels and parameters.            Furthermore,

5         Applicants mitigate various safety risks that may be associated with their electric

6         facilities through programs included in plans submitted to the Commission for

7         approval and oversight, including their respective Wildfire Mitigation Plans,

8         Emergency Operations Plans, and System Resiliency Plans. Together, these

9         measures greatly mitigate any potential fire risk associated with transmission lines

10        owned and operated by the Applicants, such as the Proposed Transmission Line

11        Project.

12               Regarding concerns related to driving, thousands of people drive under

13        transmission lines owned and operated by Applicants every day across Texas

14        without incident. The engineering design of the Proposed Transmission Line

15        Project will accommodate clearances that meet or exceed industry standards and

16        applicable regulations. These clearances provide sufficient space for cars to safely

17        park and travel underneath the transmission line.

18               Applicants’ transmission lines are designed with static wires that protect the

19        conductors from a direct lightning strike by transferring the energy of a lightning

20        strike directly to grounded components of the transmission line system. The

21        energy from the lightning strike is transferred into the ground through the structure

22        foundations and grounding wires attached to those structures. That energy is

 1         dissipated in all directions through the earth, leaving the structure at depths

2         equivalent to the depth of the structure’s foundation, typically 15 to 50 feet. This

3         varies depending on foundation depth and the resistivity of the soil layers at each

4         level of the foundation. Similarly, Applicants design their transmission lines with

5         high-speed relaying equipment that de-energizes the conductor within a few

6         milliseconds of a large lightning strike that bypasses this system.

7                Regarding arcing concerns, large arcs occur when the voltage on a power

8         line exceeds the electrical resistance properties of transmission line components

9         called insulators, as well as the insulating properties of the air surrounding the

10        energized wires. Applicants design their respective transmission lines to withstand

11        a variety of voltage conditions. As part of the Proposed Transmission Line Project,

12        Applicants performed insulation coordination studies to determine the design

13        parameters for line insulation. Applicants then used those studies to design a

14        transmission line insulation system (composed of both insulators and sufficient air

15        gap) to withstand all voltage and mechanical stresses resulting from system design

16        parameters related to power frequency, switching, and lightning surge at each

17        voltage that mitigate against flashovers, arcing, or other such electrical

18        phenomena within industry accepted levels. Additionally, the transmission line

19        structures are designed to meet or exceed national codes and standards relating

20        to phase to ground and phase to phase clearances with these electrical

21        phenomena in mind.       For further discussion on arcing, refer to the rebuttal

22        testimony of Mr. Dave Elliott.

 1         REGARDING THE STABILITY OF LAND SURROUNDING STRUCTURES AND

2         ACCESS TO AREAS OF ROUGH OR DIFFICULT TERRAIN.

3    A.   Applicants’ respective construction practices have been successfully used across

4         Texas in areas with varying terrain and geologic features to establish stable

5         foundations that support its transmission structures. Excavations during

6         construction can provide temporary opportunities for groundwater to flow into the

7         open hole during or shortly after excavation. To address this, during the installation

8         of the structure foundation, any such water is removed to prevent mixture with (and

9         dilution of) the concrete. In areas where high groundwater inflow is anticipated,

10        measures such as casing in areas with fractured rock and/or use of bentonite slurry

11        in areas with loose/flowing soils can be employed to either seal the excavation hole

12        or create enough seepage pressure to prevent groundwater inflow. Due to the

13        limited scale of transmission line foundations, potential risks to stability from

14        groundwater and moisture movement are generally not considered to be issues in

15        projects such as this. There are no codes, laws, or guidelines covering this specific

16        issue to Applicants’ knowledge and Applicants have not experienced issues with

17        their transmission line foundations affecting land stability.

18               Applicants will evaluate each individual structure location following route

19        approval to determine appropriate access methods for construction and long-term

20        maintenance activities. The use of helicopters may be considered in locations with

21        extremely rugged terrain where conventional construction equipment is not

22        feasible or practicable.

 1    Q.   IN HER TESTIMONY, INTERVENOR DONNA BAKER, M.D. (PAGE 12, LINES

2         15 THROUGH 21) NOTES THAT THERE ARE EXISTING CAVES IN THE

3         PROJECT      AREA     THAT     MAY    BE    CROSSED       BY   THE    PROPOSED

4         TRANSMISSION LINE. HOW DO APPLICANTS ADDRESS A CAVE, KARST,

5         OR SIMILAR FEATURE BEING LOCATED IN THE ROW?

6    A.   Applicants would first try to avoid potential adverse impacts to a cave, karst, or

7         cistern by spanning the subsurface feature. If avoidance is not feasible, Applicants

8         would employ practices focused on minimizing and remediating potential impacts.

9         The discovery of such a feature does not prevent the construction of transmission

10        facilities, but does require specialized, prudent construction operations. When

11        cisterns, caves, or other subsurface voids are identified near planned construction

12        activities, Applicants’ standard practices are to evaluate potential risks and

13        implement appropriate protective measures. This process is coordinated with

14        qualified professionals and performed in compliance with all applicable laws,

15        regulations, and engineering standards.

16               Where construction activities occur near caves or voids, Applicants may

17        engage a qualified geologist to observe drilling operations and assess potential

18        impacts. Vibration monitoring can be and has been implemented during drilling

19        with monitoring locations established between the drilling activity and anticipated

20        sensitive features. By utilizing engineering expertise, maintaining strict sediment

21        controls, and cooperating with the landowner, the impacts can be effectively

22        managed and minimized.

4         THE V8 LANDOWNERS COALITION (PAGE 18, LINES 11 THROUGH 15), AND

7         HAY PRODUCTION, CATTLE GRAZING, FARMING, RANCHING, AND

10        available for farming, ranching, or agricultural operations. The only areas where

11        typical farming or ranching activities may be precluded are within a structure’s

12        footprint. The 765 kV steel lattice tower that will primarily be used for the Proposed

13        Transmission Line Project generally allows for a typical span length of

14        approximately 1,400–1,500 feet.        These lattice towers therefore allow the

15        Proposed Transmission Line Project to span longer lengths compared to structures

16        designed for lower voltages, and the ROW not occupied by the base of the project’s

17        structures may still be used for other activities, such as farming, ranching, and

18        agricultural operations.

19               In Applicants’ experience, landowners are generally able to conduct their

20        agricultural and cattle operations during construction of a new transmission line.

21        The impacts of transmission line construction to harvesting crops varies depending

22        on the season of construction. Similarly, Applicants’ respective construction of
